_meta.gerado_por: scripts em dadosR6/scripts. Copiados de dadosR5/scripts SEM mudar a lógica: baixa.py, totext.py, lib.py, wikt.py, wt3.py, decl.py, verbos.py, frases.py, wp5.py (só as funções secao e it; o corte de linha passou de 2500 para 6000 caracteres), valida.py (só o nome do JSON), adj.py e pron.py (copiados e NÃO usados). grade.py copiado com UMA mudança: rótulo de caso que ocupa duas colunas (colspan=2, tabelas de полтора e оба) passou a contar como coluna de rótulo; antes criava uma coluna "forma" vazia. Novos: prep6.py (listas e cópia dos HTML já baixados), ger.py (verbete genérico: árvore de definições com marca de caso e exemplos por definição, notas de uso, formas alternativas, tabelas pela grade), sec6.py (seções 1 a 6), wp6.py (Wikipedia), frases6.py (chama frases.py), copia_r4.py (copia casos_wikipedia/preposicoes de dadosR4), final6.py (este). Ordem: prep6 → baixa → copia_r4 → totext → sec6 → wp6 → frases6 → final6 → valida.
_meta.regra: todo dado é {valor, valor_texto, unidade, fonte, url, arquivo, trecho, obs}; valor (ou cada elemento, se for lista) é fatia literal do trecho; trecho é linha literal (ou começo de linha, quando cortada) do texto extraído do arquivo; dado não achado = valor null com o motivo em obs; nada foi corrigido nem completado de memória. Campos que NÃO são item (verbete, entrada, nivel, tipo, n_caracteres, termina_em_pontuacao, etimologia, colunas, grade_expandida, criterio, subsecao, secao, secoes_do_verbete, contagem_de_exemplos, aviso, obs soltos) são rótulos ou ajudas calculadas pelo script.
_meta.texto_extraido: cada paginas/X.html (action=render da página) vira txt/X.txt com totext.py: uma linha por bloco de texto e uma linha por linha de tabela, células separadas por " | ". Células mescladas (colspan/rowspan) aparecem uma vez só no txt; por isso as tabelas de declinação e as da Wikipedia trazem também "grade_expandida" (a posição vem dos atributos do HTML).
_meta.campo_arquivo: nome do HTML em dadosR6/paginas; o txt correspondente está em dadosR6/txt (verbetes com espaço: wt_потому_что.html, wt_так_как.html, wt_то_есть.html)

verbos_de_movimento: mesmo formato de dadosR5/verbos (verbos.py), por entrada Verb: forma_acentuada, aspecto, par_aspectual, glosa, glosas_seguintes, definicoes, regencia, ipa, conjugacao (presente e futuro nas 6 pessoas, passado m/f/n/pl, imperativo sg/pl, particípios, título, notas). Acrescentados: arvore_de_definicoes (definições com os exemplos de cada uma), marcas_de_direcao, counterpart, perfectivo_correspondente_na_nota e frase_de_direcao.

verbos_de_movimento: as palavras unidirectional/multidirectional NÃO estão na linha do verbete de nenhum dos 30; elas vêm da nota de uso ("The imperfective verb идти́ ... is a unidirectional verb. Its multidirectional counterpart is ходи́ть"). A MESMA frase aparece na página do perfectivo com по- (пойти, поехать): lá ela fala do imperfectivo, não do verbete; por isso frase_de_direcao traz o campo 'verbo' (de quem a frase fala). 'marcas_de_direcao' lista toda linha da entrada que contém uma das seis palavras: ler o trecho antes de atribuir a marca ao verbo. 'abstract'/'concrete' só aparecem em ездить (em exemplos e na nota de uso). 'determinate'/'indeterminate' não aparecem em nenhum dos 30.

verbos_de_movimento: водить não tem par aspectual na linha do verbete (null). Os 12 verbos prefixados (прийти, приходить, уйти, уходить, войти, входить, выйти, выходить, приехать, приезжать, уехать, уезжать) não têm marca de direção nem counterpart: null com motivo.
verbos_de_movimento: уходить e выходить têm DUAS entradas Verb (homógrafos: уходи́ть pf 'to exhaust'; вы́ходить pf 'to rear', com acento diferente). Usar a entrada 0 para o verbo de movimento.

verbos_de_movimento: ехать tem QUATRO formas de imperativo na célula (поезжа́й, езжа́й, е́хай, е́дь), duas com marca 2△; приехать tem duas (приезжа́й, прие́дь △*); a legenda das marcas está em conjugacao/notas. Não escolher forma sem ler a nota. Perfectivos não têm presente (células com travessão = null).

verbos_de_movimento/wikipedia: os exemplos da seção "Verbs of motion" de Russian grammar vêm SEM acento (Мы идём в библиотеку.) e, na tabela de prefixos, o prefixo vem separado do verbo por espaço ("во шла", "при ехал"): é assim no texto extraído (a página destaca o prefixo); não juntar sem dizer. A regra de caso/preposição por prefixo está na 3ª coluna da tabela "Prefixed verbs of motion" (ex.: "в / на + acc."), literal. Só a tabela de pares traz os verbos com acento.

preposicoes: só as entradas Preposition foram guardadas (as outras classes do verbete estão listadas em entradas_da_secao_russa e em _meta/avisos_calculados). A marca de caso vem de DOIS jeitos, conforme a página: (1) na linha do verbete (regencia_na_linha_do_verbete, ex.: к '[with dative]'), valendo para a entrada inteira; (2) como item-mãe da lista de definições (в, на, с, о, по, за, под: a definição de nível 1 é só '[with accusative]' e os sentidos são as subdefinicoes, que trazem 'marcas_de_caso_da_definicao_mae'). Há também marcas dentro do texto de uma definição.

preposicoes: as variantes во, со, ко, об, обо, изо, ото, подо, передо NÃO vêm na linha do verbete: vêm em 'formas_alternativas' (subseção Alternative forms) e/ou nas notas de uso, com a condição de uso literal. A forma de antes de 1918 (въ, съ...) aparece na mesma lista.

preposicoes: as listas por caso da Wikipedia (cópia de dadosR4) não são completas e trazem as preposições sem acento; a comparação com o Wiktionary está em divergencias (за no nominativo) e em _meta/avisos_calculados.

numerais: todas as entradas da seção Russian foram guardadas (inclusive homógrafos sem relação: три e пять como imperativo de verbo, сорок como genitivo plural de соро́ка, шестой/седьмой/восьмой como forma de substantivo). Filtrar por 'classe'.

numerais: a classe NÃO é sempre Numeral: ноль e половина são Noun; первый...десятый são Adjective; сколько e несколько têm entrada Pronoun e Adverb; много e мало são Adverb (sem tabela de declinação na página). тысяча tem entrada Numeral e entrada Noun.

numerais: as tabelas de declinação têm estruturas diferentes; a lista completa (colunas e título de cada uma) está em _meta/avisos_calculados/estrutura_das_tabelas_de_declinacao. Resumo: один = masculine, neuter, feminine, plural; два = masculine/neuter, feminine; три, четыре, пять...тридцать = uma coluna chamada 'singular' pela página; восемь, сорок, пятьдесят...девяносто = uma coluna SEM cabeçalho (chamada 'forma' pelo script); сто = singular, plural (o plural só tem genitivo со́т); двести...пятьсот = uma coluna 'plural'; тысяча, миллион, ноль, половина = singular, plural; полтора = masculine/neuter, feminine; оба = masculine, neuter, feminine, m./n. plural, f. plural (as três primeiras quase todas com travessão); ordinais = masculine, neuter, feminine, plural. Nas tabelas com linhas animate/inanimate o acusativo é {animate, inanimate}.

numerais: no Wiktionary as tabelas acentuam monossílabos (пя́ть, три́, сто́) e a linha do verbete não (пять); a Wikipedia também não. Essas diferenças estão em _meta/avisos_calculados (só acento em monossílabo), não em divergencias.

numerais: o caso do substantivo depois do numeral está nas 'notas_de_uso' de cada verbete (один: nos exemplos da definição; два/три/четыре; пять...; сто; тысяча) e nas seções da Wikipedia. As notas de два têm 35 linhas, com exemplos em três linhas seguidas (russo, transliteração, tradução). A página de два traz um aviso de limpeza ("Usage notes are not in a good format").

numerais/wikipedia: o título "Russian numerals" é redirecionamento para "Russian declension"; não existe artigo separado. A tabela de 200–900 de Russian declension traz 'трeмяста́ми' com um 'e' LATINO no meio (está em avisos_calculados). Os exemplos 'один рубль', 'десять рублей' vêm sem acento.

tempo: formato de dadosR4/declinacoes (decl.py) no nível do verbete (primeira entrada Noun: genero, genitivo, nominativo_plural, genitivo_plural, tabela), mais 'entradas' (todas as classes, com a árvore de definições e os exemplos) e 'linhas_com_expressao_de_tempo' (busca por expressão regular; pode trazer linha que não é de tempo). A lista pedida tinha 39 palavras (não 40). сейчас não tem entrada Noun; сегодня, завтра e вчера têm Noun indeclinável (sem tabela) e Adverb.

tempo: NENHUMA página de dia da semana ou de mês traz nota de uso dizendo 'в + acusativo' ou 'в + preposicional'. O que existe são exemplos (в понеде́льник ― on Monday; по понеде́льникам ― on Mondays; в январе́ ― in January), sem nome de caso. A regra escrita está no verbete da preposição в: '[with accusative]' → '(time) at, in, on' com o exemplo 'в пя́тницу ― on Friday'; para 'in January' com o preposicional não há frase de regra em nenhuma página coletada (o caso de январе́ se confere na tabela de declinação de январь).

tempo: notas de uso úteis: час (acento em два часа́), год (лет depois de numeral), утро (acento), век, месяц. среда e век têm duas entradas Noun (среда́ 'Wednesday' é a usada; a outra é 'environment').

imperativo_e_condicional/wikipedia: as seções coletadas falam de -и, -ь, -й, -те, da negação com не e do condicional com бы + passado. NÃO falam de давай/давайте nem de пусть, nem da escolha de aspecto no imperativo negado, nem da posição de бы além de 'after the word which marks the supposed subject' (Russian grammar) e 'usually follows the verb' (Conditional mood): as duas frases estão guardadas, sem escolher. Para давай, давайте, пусть, чтобы, если e бы usar os verbetes do Wiktionary (definições com '[with imperfective infinitive]', '[with perfective first-person plural future]' e exemplos). A página Subjunctive mood não tem seção de russo (só polonês e búlgaro) e não foi guardada como seção.

imperativo_e_condicional/wikipedia: na tabela do imperativo de Russian grammar a terminação vem separada por espaço ('де́ла й те'); os exemplos da página Imperative mood vêm sem acento e com notação própria (читаj-у — читай).

conjuncoes: todas as entradas de cada verbete foram guardadas (inclusive letra, substantivo, interjeição); filtrar por 'classe'. A classe varia: тоже, также, поэтому, однако, зато, то есть, куда, откуда, почему, зачем são Adverb no Wiktionary (não Conjunction); когда, где, как, пока têm entrada Adverb e Conjunction; который é Pronoun (tabela de tipo adjetivo: masculine, neuter, feminine, plural); что tem tabela de pronome com uma coluna. потому что, так как e поэтому não têm nenhum exemplo com tradução na página.

conjuncoes/wikipedia: a seção Syntax de Russian grammar (ordem das palavras, negação, coordenação, subordinação) traz os exemplos SEM acento e as conjunções da lista de subordinação com transcrição entre colchetes. Não existe seção chamada 'Conjunctions' nem 'Word order' (a ordem das palavras está no começo de Syntax).

frases: todas as frases com tradução de até 70 caracteres (contados sem o acento) das páginas das seções 1 a 6, de qualquer subseção da seção Russian (definições, notas de uso etc.), sem repetição exata; 'classe_da_entrada' e 'entrada' dizem de que entrada vieram, 'subsecao' diz se vieram de Usage notes. Muitas são sintagmas e não orações: usar 'termina_em_pontuacao'. Exemplos sem tradução e os não localizados no texto extraído ficaram de fora (contagem em _meta).

Os exemplos também aparecem dentro de cada definição (campo 'exemplos' da árvore), sem limite de tamanho; ali a citação literária traz 'citacao_fonte'. Em 'frases' a citação traz 'citacao' {fonte, ano, autor}.

Células com '-' ou '—' = a página não dá a forma (null com motivo). 'valor' em lista = a célula traz duas ou mais formas, na ordem da página; marcas (* △ algarismos) ficam no obs e a legenda em 'notas'.

notas_de_uso.valor: The imperative forms едь (jedʹ) / е́дьте (jédʹte) and е́хай (jéxaj) / е́хайте (jéxajte) (including derivatives with prefixes) are used but are considered illiterate and are not recommended for use. The recommended imperative forms are suppletive forms поезжа́й (pojezžáj) / поезжа́йте (pojezžájte) but езжа́й (jezžáj) / езжа́йте (jezžájte) are also acceptable. The derivatives (приезжать, заезжать, выезжать, etc.) use prefix + езжа́й (jezžáj) / prefix + езжа́йте (jezžájte). For negative imperative, use не е́зди (ne jézdi).

russo.valor: — Росси́я вас не забу́дет! — ря́вкнул Остап. Ипполит Матвеевич, держа́ в руке́ сла́дкий пирожо́к, с недоуме́нием слу́шал Остапа, но удержа́ть его́ бы́ло нельзя́. Его́ несло́. Великий комбина́тор чу́вствовал вдохнове́ние, упои́тельное состоя́ние перед вышесредним шантажо́м. Он прошелся по ко́мнате, как барс.

transliteracao.valor: — Rossíja vas ne zabúdet! — rjávknul Ostap. Ippolit Matvejevič, deržá v ruké sládkij pirožók, s nedouménijem slúšal Ostapa, no uderžátʹ jevó býlo nelʹzjá. Jevó nesló. Velikij kombinátor čúvstvoval vdoxnovénije, upoítelʹnoje sostojánije pered vyšesrednim šantažóm. On prošelsja po kómnate, kak bars.

traducao.valor: "Russia will never forget you!" bellowed Ostap. Ippolit Matveyevich, holding a sweet bun in his hand, listened to Ostap in perplexity but was unable to hold him. He was carried away. The great combinator felt inspiration, ravishing condition before the upper-middle class blackmailing. He paced through the room like a leopard

titulo.valor_texto: ### Verbs of motion
titulo.trecho: ### Verbs of motion
titulo.obs: título da seção

linha.valor: Verbs of motion are a distinct class of verbs found in several Slavic languages. Due to the extensive semantic information they contain, Russian verbs of motion pose difficulties for non-native learners at all levels of study.[21] Unprefixed verbs of motion, which are all imperfective, divide into pairs based on the direction of the movement (uni- or multidirectional — sometimes referred to as determinate/indeterminate or definite/indefinite). As opposed to a verb-framed language, in which path is encoded in the verb, but manner of motion typically is expressed with complements, Russian is a satellite language, meaning that these concepts are encoded in both the root of the verb and the particles associated with it, satellites.[22] Thus, the roots of motion verbs convey the lexical information of manner of movement, e.g. walking, crawling, running, whereas prefixes denote path, e.g. motion in and out of space.[23][note 1] The roots also distinguish between means of conveyance, e.g. by transport or by one's own power, and in transitive verbs, the object or person being transported.[24] The information below provides an outline of the formation and basic usage of unprefixed and prefixed verbs of motion.

linha.valor: Motion verbs combine with prefixes to form new aspectual pairs, which lose the distinction of directionality, but gain spatial or temporal meanings. The unidirectional verb serves as the base for the perfective, and the multidirectional as the base for the imperfective. In addition to the meanings conveyed by the prefix and the simplex motion verb, prepositional phrases also contribute to the expression of path in Russian.[26] Thus, it is important to consider the whole verb phrase when examining verbs of motion.

linhas: в-, во- Movement inwards across a threshold, entering Antonym: вы-
The tram stopped and the girl entered. Трамвай остановился, и девушка во шла.
вы- Movement out of something across a threshold, exiting Antonym: в-

She exited the office. Она вы шла из кабинета. Other: Step out for a short period of time, e.g.: The secretary left for ten minutes. Секретарь вы шел на десять минут. Leave at a specific time frame, e.g.: They left early in the morning to catch their train/plane . Они вы ехали рано утром, чтобы успеть на поезд/самолёт.
из / с / от + gen. в / на + acc. к + dat.
при- Intended arrival, signals presence of the agent at a location as a result of motion Antonym: у-
He arrived in Moscow a week ago. Он при ехал в Москву неделю назад.
в / на + acc. к + dat. из / с / от + gen.
у- Intended departure, signals absence Antonym: при-
They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Они у летят из Владивостока через месяц. Where is Igor? He already left. Где Игорь? Он уже у шёл.
в / на + acc. к + dat. из / с / от + gen.
He approached the girl to ask for her number. Он подо шёл к девушке, чтобы спросить её номер. Other: Под везти – give someone a lift, e.g.: He took me (as far as) downtown. Он под вёз меня до центра.
от-, ото- Withdrawal a short distance away Antonym: под-

The boy stepped back from the stranger who had offered him candy. Мальчик ото шёл от незнакомца, который предложил ему конфеты. Other: With transitive verbs, delivering or dropping something off (agent does not remain), e.g.: I'll drop the book off at the library, then come. Я от несу книги в библиотеку, потом приду.
до- Reaching a limit or destination

The passengers reached the last station and exited the bus. Пассажиры до ехали до последней остановки и вышли из автобуса. Other: Characterizing the duration of a journey, especially when it is long, e.g.: We finally reached the dacha. Мы наконец до ехали до дачи.
за- Movement behind an object; stopping off on the way

The old woman walked behind the corner and disappeared. Старушка за шла за угол и исчезла. Other: Action performed on the way to a destination, e.g.: On the way home I stopped at the store for bread. По дороге домой я за шла в магазин за хлебом A short visit, e.g.: The young man often stops by his mother's place. Молодой человек часто за ходит к маме. Movement deep into something, at a great distance (inside, upwards or downwards), e.g.: The ball flew onto the roof of the house. Мяч за летел на крышу дома.
в / на / за + acc. к + dat. за + inst.
про- Movement across, through, or past something

We drove through the city. Мы про ехали через город. We passed the metro station. Мы про шли мимо станции метро. Other: Movement beyond one's destination (possibly unintentional), e.g.: I'm afraid we already passed the store. Я боюсь, что мы уже про шли магазин. Movement forward with the distance covered specified, e.g.: You'll go three stops and get off the tram. Вы про едете три остановки и выйдете из трамвая.
сквозь / через / в + acc. мимо + gen. without preposition
пере- Movement across, from one point to another; through
The ducks swam across the river. Утки пере плыли реку. Other: Changing residence, e.g.: I moved to another city. Я пере ехала в другой город.
вз-, взо-, воз-, вс-, вос- Movement upwards Antonym: с-
The mountain climber walked up the mountain. Альпинист взо шёл на гору.
с-, со- Movement downwards Antonym: вз-
After the performance, the actor got off the stage. После представления актёр со шёл со сцены.
c + gen. на + acc. к + dat. за + inst.
о-, об-, обо- Movement around an object or involving a consecutive number of objects, circling, covering a whole place
The little girl walked around the puddle. Девочка обо шла лужу. I'm going around to all the stores in the mall. Я об хожу все магазины в центре.

linhas: It's snowing, not raining. Идёт не дождь, а снег. The clock is ticking. Часы идут. A film is on. Идёт фильм. That dress suits you. Это платье тебе идёт. The government is moving towards democracy. Правительство идёт к демократии. The president is going against the will of the people. Президент идёт против воли народа.

The country is waging a war. Страна ведёт войну. The girl keeps a diary. Девочка ведёт дневник. The friends have been in correspondence for a long time. Друзья долго ведут переписку. The road leads to the city. Дорога ведёт в город. No good comes from lying. Ложь к добру не ведёт.

The woman bears the responsibility of her children. Женщина несёт ответственность за детей. The farmer bears the losses from the drought. Фермер несёт потери от засухи. The criminal is undergoing severe punishment. Преступник несёт тяжёлое наказание. The speaker is talking nonsense. Оратор несёт чушь.
Time flies. Время летит. Shares are plummeting because of the economic crisis. Акции летят от экономического кризиса.
The hooligans are getting into a brawl. Хулиганы лезут в драку.
She is lucky/got lucky. Ей везёт / повезло.
Blood is flowing from the wound. Кровь бежит из раны. The days fly past. Дни бегут.

linha.valor: Verbs of motion are a distinct class of verbs found in several Slavic languages. Due to the extensive semantic information they contain, Russian verbs of motion pose difficulties for non-native learners at all levels of study.[21] Unprefixed verbs of motion, which are all imperfective, divide into pairs based on the direction of the movement (uni- or multidirectional — sometimes referred to as determinate/indeterminate or definite/indefinite). As opposed to a verb-framed language, in which path is encoded in the verb, but manner of motion typically is expressed with complements, Russian is a satellite language, meaning that these concepts are encoded in both the root of the verb and the particles associated with it, satellites.[22] Thus, the roots of motion verbs convey the lexical information of manner of movement, e.g. walking, crawling, running, whereas prefixes denote path, e.g. motion in and out of space.[23][note 1] The roots also distinguish between means of conveyance, e.g. by transport or by one's own power, and in transitive verbs, the object or person being transported.[24] The information below provides an outline of the formation and basic usage of unprefixed and prefixed verbs of motion.

linha.valor: Motion verbs combine with prefixes to form new aspectual pairs, which lose the distinction of directionality, but gain spatial or temporal meanings. The unidirectional verb serves as the base for the perfective, and the multidirectional as the base for the imperfective. In addition to the meanings conveyed by the prefix and the simplex motion verb, prepositional phrases also contribute to the expression of path in Russian.[26] Thus, it is important to consider the whole verb phrase when examining verbs of motion.

linha.valor: Verbs of motion are a distinct class of verbs found in several Slavic languages. Due to the extensive semantic information they contain, Russian verbs of motion pose difficulties for non-native learners at all levels of study.[21] Unprefixed verbs of motion, which are all imperfective, divide into pairs based on the direction of the movement (uni- or multidirectional — sometimes referred to as determinate/indeterminate or definite/indefinite). As opposed to a verb-framed language, in which path is encoded in the verb, but manner of motion typically is expressed with complements, Russian is a satellite language, meaning that these concepts are encoded in both the root of the verb and the particles associated with it, satellites.[22] Thus, the roots of motion verbs convey the lexical information of manner of movement, e.g. walking, crawling, running, whereas prefixes denote path, e.g. motion in and out of space.[23][note 1] The roots also distinguish between means of conveyance, e.g. by transport or by one's own power, and in transitive verbs, the object or person being transported.[24] The information below provides an outline of the formation and basic usage of unprefixed and prefixed verbs of motion.

linha.valor: Motion verbs combine with prefixes to form new aspectual pairs, which lose the distinction of directionality, but gain spatial or temporal meanings. The unidirectional verb serves as the base for the perfective, and the multidirectional as the base for the imperfective. In addition to the meanings conveyed by the prefix and the simplex motion verb, prepositional phrases also contribute to the expression of path in Russian.[26] Thus, it is important to consider the whole verb phrase when examining verbs of motion.

linha.valor: Motion verbs combine with prefixes to form new aspectual pairs, which lose the distinction of directionality, but gain spatial or temporal meanings. The unidirectional verb serves as the base for the perfective, and the multidirectional as the base for the imperfective. In addition to the meanings conveyed by the prefix and the simplex motion verb, prepositional phrases also contribute to the expression of path in Russian.[26] Thus, it is important to consider the whole verb phrase when examining verbs of motion.

notas_de_uso.valor: Sentences with пе́ред са́мым (péred sámym) use perfective verbs. Compared to sentences with perfective verbs while using the ordinary пе́ред (péred), it has a much shorter interval between the completed action/event and the particular action/event that the пе́ред са́мым (péred sámym) modifies. Hence, пе́ред са́мым (péred sámym) has a bigger emphasis meaning-wise than the ordinary пе́ред (péred).

linhas.valor: In Russian, accusative is used not only to display the direct object of an action, but also to indicate the destination or goal of motion. It is also used with some prepositions. linhas.valor: In Russian, the dative case is used for indicating the indirect object of an action (that to which something is given, thrown, read, etc.). In the instance where a person is the goal of motion, dative is used instead of accusative to indicate motion toward. This is usually achieved with the preposition κ + destination in dative case; К врачу, meaning "to the doctor."

In the instance where a person is the goal of motion, dative is used instead of accusative to indicate motion toward. This is usually achieved with the preposition κ + destination in dative case; К врачу, meaning "to the doctor."

linhas.valor: In grammar, the prepositional case (abbreviated prep) and the postpositional case (abbreviated post) - generalised as adpositional cases - are grammatical cases that respectively mark the object of a preposition and a postposition. This term can be used in languages where nouns have a declensional form that appears exclusively in combination with certain prepositions.

notas_de_uso.valor: The reason behind the genitive singular here is that in Old Russian два governed the dual number, and the old nominative dual form was the same as the masculine genitive singular. When the dual number was lost in Russian, the form was reanalyzed as the genitive singular. This was extended to include the numbers три (tri) and четы́ре (četýre), and eventually it was applied by analogy to feminine nouns as well.

notas_de_uso.valor: Тысяча in all cases governs the genitive plural of the noun, except for instrumental case. In instrumental case, тысяча can potentially function either as a numeral (with the form тысячью, in which case the noun must also be in instrumental case) or as a noun (with the form тысячей, in which case the following noun is in genitive plural). However, not all Russians recognize this distinction and may use both indiscriminately.

linha.valor: Different Russian numerals have very different types of declension. The word оди́н (one) is declined by number, gender (in the singular), and case. The word два (two) is declined by gender and case, all other numbers have only case to decline by. The words for 50, 60, 70, 80, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 are unique for Russian, as they decline not only with ending in their end, but also with part of word in their middle (since they are originally composed from two words): Nom. пятьдеся́т (50) – Gen. пяти́десяти etc. (compare пять деся́тков – пяти́ деся́тков "five tens").

linha.valor: Compound number phrases are created without any unions: сто пятьдеся́т три ры́бы "153 fish". All numerals are declined concurrently, albeit not always in the spoken language. If numeral is in Nominative or Accusative, ending of the noun is defined by the last numeral word (the least order, see examples below), but this may not be true for an adjective attached to this noun.[17]

linha.valor: Most numbers ending with "1" (in any gender: оди́н, одна́, одно́) require Nominative singular for a noun: два́дцать одна́ маши́на (21 cars), сто пятьдеся́т оди́н челове́к (151 people). Most numbers ending with "2", "3", "4" (два/две, три, четы́ре) require Genitive singular: три соба́ки (3 dogs), со́рок два окна́ (42 windows). All other numbers (including 0 and those ending with it) require Genitive plural: пять я́блок (5 apples), де́сять рубле́й (10 rubles). Genitive plural is also used for numbers ending with 11 to 14 and with inexact numerals: сто оди́ннадцать ме́тров (111 meters); мно́го домо́в (many houses). Nominative plural is used only without numerals: э́ти дома́ (these houses); cf. три до́ма (3 houses; G. sg.). These rules apply only for integer numbers.[18] For rational numbers see below.

linha.valor: In oblique cases, noun and number take both this case, except that the numbers ending with "thousand", "million", "billion" etc. (nouns: ты́сяча (f.), миллио́н (m.), миллиа́рд (m.)) in singular or in plural are regarded as nouns and always require Genitive case in plural: пятью́ ты́сячами (Instr.) маши́н (Gen.); cf. пятью́ маши́нами and пятью́ ты́сячами тремяста́ми маши́нами (all Instr.). Initial (leftmost) numeral "1" can be omitted in combinations (одна́) ты́сяча (ты́сяча и одна́ ночь – 1001 nights), (оди́н) миллио́н, etc.

linha.valor: Nouns со́тня ("approximately 100", f.) and па́ра ("pair", f.) can be declined and can form compound numerals: три со́тни (≈ 300), пять пар носко́в (5 pair of socks). Approximate numbers are colloquially formed by reversing word order, exchanging numeral and noun: мину́ты три (≈3 minutes). Ranges (hyphenated) are also possible: пять-шесть дней (5–6 days), дней пять-шесть (probably 5–6 days). The word ми́нус (minus) declines if standalone, but does not for negative numbers: минус три гра́дуса – minus three degrees (wrong: *минуса три градуса); however: три минуса – three minuses.

linha.valor: For numbers above 1,000 Russian uses a modified short scale with the following loanwords: миллио́н (106, million; as for both long and short scales), миллиа́рд (109, milliard; as for long scale – an exception), триллио́н (1012, trillion), квадриллио́н (1015, quadrillion), квинтиллио́н (1018, quintillion), etc. (continued as short scale). They decline in the same way as миллио́н. Russian uses words биллио́н (billion) and numerals with -ard endings only in historical texts or literal translations. Also, биллиа́рд (billiard) is a noun meaning a cue sport.

linha.valor: Collective numerals (Russian: собира́тельные числи́тельные) are used in Russian (and many other Slavic languages) instead of usual cardinal ones in specific lexical and semantic situations. Russian collective numerals are different from the cardinal numerals in that the former emphasize ‘the totality’ or ‘the aggregate as a whole’, while the latter – ‘the individuated quantity’.[19] Only numerals from 2 (двое) to 7 (семеро) are actively used nowadays, while 8 to 10 are seldom used and 11–13 are not normative;[20] word о́ба (both) is also considered to be collective numeral.[19] In nominative and accusative, they always force the noun into genitive plural form (while their own accusative form is dependent on the animacy of the noun): трое друзей на охоту пошли, вижу двоих мужчин, вижу двое саней. (Three friends went hunting [together], I see two men [together], I see two sleighs [together].) These numerals are seldom used in oblique cases, especially instrumental.[20] A brief table of usage situations follows:

linha.valor: Ordinal numbers have grammatically no differences with adjectives. While forming them, upper three orders of numerals are agglutinated to nearest dividing power of 1000, which results in constructing some of the longest natural Russian words, e.g. стапятидесятитрёхты́сячный (153,000-th), while the next is сто пятьдеся́т три ты́сячи пе́рвый (153,001-st). In the latter example, only the last word is declined with noun.

linha.valor: Fractions are formed as: (how much parts), expressed by cardinal number in case of the phrase, plus (of how numerous parts), expressed by ordinal number; the construction is formed as like it were related to word часть "part" (grammatically feminine), which is usually omitted. Noun to such construction always comes in Genitive single, also as like it belonged to word часть: девяно́сто две пятидеся́тых то́нны "+92⁄50 tons". If an integer precedes a fraction, it is bound to it usually with the conjunction и, while the noun remains in Genitive: два и три восьмы́х оборо́та "2+3⁄8 turns" (оборо́т is masculine, so the numeral is два, not *две).

linha.valor: Fractions +1⁄2, +1⁄3 and +1⁄4 have proper names (nouns): полови́на, треть and че́тверть, which are used instead of ordinal numbers. They are also often added with preposition с, while form of noun appears to be related to the integer part rather than to the fraction: де́сять с че́твертью [Instr.] оборо́тов [Gen.] "10+1⁄4 turns". Prefixes пол- (with Genitive) and полу- (with Nominative) are used for "half" of something: пол-лимо́на (half of a lemon), полчаса́ (half an hour; but: полови́на ча́са); полуме́сяц (half moon, crescent). Words with пол- are not declined, and there is a set of rules for writing with or without dash.

linha.valor: For "1+1⁄2" there is a special word полтора́ (feminine полторы́; in oblique cases полу́тора; requires Genitive): полтора́ я́блока – +3⁄2 apples. It can be used with larger numbers (полторы́ ты́сячи – 1 500, полтора миллио́на – 1 500 000) and, for approximate values, with smaller numbers (полтора деся́тка – ≈ 15, полторы со́тни – ≈ 150). There was also now-outdated form полтора́ста for exactly 150. As with other single-word numerals, it's possible to form nouns and multiplicative adjectives, associated with "1.5": полу́торка (old truck with 1.5 tonnes of payload capacity), полтора́шка (1.5 liter plastic bottle for beverage); полу́торный (something of 150% amount). Also (colloquially): полтора́ челове́ка "almost nobody" (lit. one and a half men).

linha.valor: To read decimal fractions,[note 3] convert them to simple ones: 2,71828 = 2 + +71828⁄100000 - два и се́мьдесят одна́ ты́сяча восемьсо́т два́дцать во́семь стоты́сячных. After integer in such cases is often used word це́лая (nominalized adjective "full, integer", which also refers to omitted word часть and thus is feminine): 3,14 – три це́лых (и) четы́рнадцать со́тых (union is often omitted); word це́лая can appear also in naming non-decimal simple fractions: 2+3⁄8 – две це́лых три восьмы́х. Zero before comma is often read: 0,01 = 0 + +1⁄100 – ноль це́лых одна́ со́тая (shortly: одна́ со́тая). Informally, decimal fractional part can be read more conveniently as sequence of simple digits and numbers: два и семь-восемна́дцать-два́дцать во́семь. Same method is used to read long numerals unrelated to a noun (phone numbers, address indexes, etc.), grouping two or three digits: 123406 – сто два́дцать три четы́реста шесть, двенадцать три́дцать четы́ре ноль шесть (forced ноль added to avoid missing digit).

linha.valor: Russian also has so-called "count form" (счётная фо́рма) for use by nouns in numerical phrases instead of genitive plural (for some words mandatory, for others optional), mainly with units of measure (especially derived from names): во́семь бит (8 bits; not *би́тов), шестна́дцать байт (16 bytes), две́сти два́дцать вольт (220 volts), пять килогра́мм(ов) (5 kilograms; optional). But: коли́чество ба́йтов (amount of bytes), изба́виться от ли́шних килогра́ммов (get rid of excess kilograms).

linha.valor: Count form also exists for paucal numbers (1.5, 2, 3 and 4); usually it coincides with genitive singular, but has notable exceptions with stressed endings: два часа́ (2 hours), but середи́на ча́са (middle of an hour); два́дцать два шара́ (22 balls), but объём ша́ра (volume of the ball); три ряда́ (3 rows/lines), but вы́йти из ря́да (step out of the line); четы́ре шага́ (4 steps), but полша́га (half a step). Полчаса́ (half an hour) is additional exception; other nouns with пол- prefix does not have stressed -а ending.

linha.valor: A few nouns have unrelated suppletive genitive plural forms: 4 го́да, but 5 лет (years); 3 челове́ка, but 30 люде́й/челове́к (people; optional). Count forms for adjectives and nouns with adjectival declension after numerals require genitive plural and nominative plural: два лу́чших (G. pl.) игрока́ (G. sg.) "2 best players"; три зелёные (N. pl.) прямы́е (N. pl.) lit. "3 green straight lines", but три зелёных (G. pl.) прямы́х (G. pl.) штриха́ (G. sg.) lit. "3 green straight strokes".

linha.valor: Different Russian numerals have very different types of declension. The word оди́н (one) is declined by number, gender (in the singular), and case. The word два (two) is declined by gender and case, all other numbers have only case to decline by. The words for 50, 60, 70, 80, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 are unique for Russian, as they decline not only with ending in their end, but also with part of word in their middle (since they are originally composed from two words): Nom. пятьдеся́т (50) – Gen. пяти́десяти etc. (compare пять деся́тков – пяти́ деся́тков "five tens").

linha.valor: Most numbers ending with "1" (in any gender: оди́н, одна́, одно́) require Nominative singular for a noun: два́дцать одна́ маши́на (21 cars), сто пятьдеся́т оди́н челове́к (151 people). Most numbers ending with "2", "3", "4" (два/две, три, четы́ре) require Genitive singular: три соба́ки (3 dogs), со́рок два окна́ (42 windows). All other numbers (including 0 and those ending with it) require Genitive plural: пять я́блок (5 apples), де́сять рубле́й (10 rubles). Genitive plural is also used for numbers ending with 11 to 14 and with inexact numerals: сто оди́ннадцать ме́тров (111 meters); мно́го домо́в (many houses). Nominative plural is used only without numerals: э́ти дома́ (these houses); cf. три до́ма (3 houses; G. sg.). These rules apply only for integer numbers.[18] For rational numbers see below.

linha.valor: Collective numerals (Russian: собира́тельные числи́тельные) are used in Russian (and many other Slavic languages) instead of usual cardinal ones in specific lexical and semantic situations. Russian collective numerals are different from the cardinal numerals in that the former emphasize ‘the totality’ or ‘the aggregate as a whole’, while the latter – ‘the individuated quantity’.[19] Only numerals from 2 (двое) to 7 (семеро) are actively used nowadays, while 8 to 10 are seldom used and 11–13 are not normative;[20] word о́ба (both) is also considered to be collective numeral.[19] In nominative and accusative, they always force the noun into genitive plural form (while their own accusative form is dependent on the animacy of the noun): трое друзей на охоту пошли, вижу двоих мужчин, вижу двое саней. (Three friends went hunting [together], I see two men [together], I see two sleighs [together].) linha.valor: Most numbers ending with "1" (in any gender: оди́н, одна́, одно́) require Nominative singular for a noun: два́дцать одна́ маши́на (21 cars), сто пятьдеся́т оди́н челове́к (151 people). Most numbers ending with "2", "3", "4" (два/две, три, четы́ре) require Genitive singular: три соба́ки (3 dogs), со́рок два окна́ (42 windows). All other numbers (including 0 and those ending with it) require Genitive plural: пять я́блок (5 apples), де́сять рубле́й (10 rubles). Genitive plural is also used for numbers ending with 11 to 14 and with inexact numerals: сто оди́ннадцать ме́тров (111 meters); мно́го домо́в (many houses). Nominative plural is used only without numerals: э́ти дома́ (these houses); cf. три до́ма (3 houses; G. sg.). These rules apply only for integer numbers.[18] For rational numbers see below.

linha.valor: Nouns со́тня ("approximately 100", f.) and па́ра ("pair", f.) can be declined and can form compound numerals: три со́тни (≈ 300), пять пар носко́в (5 pair of socks). Approximate numbers are colloquially formed by reversing word order, exchanging numeral and noun: мину́ты три (≈3 minutes). Ranges (hyphenated) are also possible: пять-шесть дней (5–6 days), дней пять-шесть (probably 5–6 days). The word ми́нус (minus) declines if standalone, but does not for negative numbers: минус три гра́дуса – minus three degrees (wrong: *минуса три градуса); however: три минуса – three minuses.

linha.valor: Ordinal numbers have grammatically no differences with adjectives. While forming them, upper three orders of numerals are agglutinated to nearest dividing power of 1000, which results in constructing some of the longest natural Russian words, e.g. стапятидесятитрёхты́сячный (153,000-th), while the next is сто пятьдеся́т три ты́сячи пе́рвый (153,001-st). In the latter example, only the last word is declined with noun.

linha.valor: To read decimal fractions,[note 3] convert them to simple ones: 2,71828 = 2 + +71828⁄100000 - два и се́мьдесят одна́ ты́сяча восемьсо́т два́дцать во́семь стоты́сячных. After integer in such cases is often used word це́лая (nominalized adjective "full, integer", which also refers to omitted word часть and thus is feminine): 3,14 – три це́лых (и) четы́рнадцать со́тых (union is often omitted); word це́лая can appear also in naming non-decimal simple fractions: 2+3⁄8 – две це́лых три восьмы́х. Zero before comma is often read: 0,01 = 0 + +1⁄100 – ноль це́лых одна́ со́тая (shortly: одна́ со́тая). Informally, decimal fractional part can be read more conveniently as sequence of simple digits and numbers: два и семь-восемна́дцать-два́дцать во́семь. Same method is used to read long numerals unrelated to a noun (phone numbers, address indexes, etc.), grouping two or three digits: 123406 – сто два́дцать три четы́реста шесть, двенадцать три́дцать четы́ре ноль шесть (forced ноль added to avoid missing digit).

linha.valor: Russian also has so-called "count form" (счётная фо́рма) for use by nouns in numerical phrases instead of genitive plural (for some words mandatory, for others optional), mainly with units of measure (especially derived from names): во́семь бит (8 bits; not *би́тов), шестна́дцать байт (16 bytes), две́сти два́дцать вольт (220 volts), пять килогра́мм(ов) (5 kilograms; optional). But: коли́чество ба́йтов (amount of bytes), изба́виться от ли́шних килогра́ммов (get rid of excess kilograms).

linha.valor: Count form also exists for paucal numbers (1.5, 2, 3 and 4); usually it coincides with genitive singular, but has notable exceptions with stressed endings: два часа́ (2 hours), but середи́на ча́са (middle of an hour); два́дцать два шара́ (22 balls), but объём ша́ра (volume of the ball); три ряда́ (3 rows/lines), but вы́йти из ря́да (step out of the line); четы́ре шага́ (4 steps), but полша́га (half a step). Полчаса́ (half an hour) is additional exception; other nouns with пол- prefix does not have stressed -а ending.

linha.valor: Different Russian numerals have very different types of declension. The word оди́н (one) is declined by number, gender (in the singular), and case. The word два (two) is declined by gender and case, all other numbers have only case to decline by. The words for 50, 60, 70, 80, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 are unique for Russian, as they decline not only with ending in their end, but also with part of word in their middle (since they are originally composed from two words): Nom. пятьдеся́т (50) – Gen. пяти́десяти etc. (compare пять деся́тков – пяти́ деся́тков "five tens").

linha.valor: Compound number phrases are created without any unions: сто пятьдеся́т три ры́бы "153 fish". All numerals are declined concurrently, albeit not always in the spoken language. If numeral is in Nominative or Accusative, ending of the noun is defined by the last numeral word (the least order, see examples below), but this may not be true for an adjective attached to this noun.[17]

linha.valor: Nouns со́тня ("approximately 100", f.) and па́ра ("pair", f.) can be declined and can form compound numerals: три со́тни (≈ 300), пять пар носко́в (5 pair of socks). Approximate numbers are colloquially formed by reversing word order, exchanging numeral and noun: мину́ты три (≈3 minutes). Ranges (hyphenated) are also possible: пять-шесть дней (5–6 days), дней пять-шесть (probably 5–6 days). The word ми́нус (minus) declines if standalone, but does not for negative numbers: минус три гра́дуса – minus three degrees (wrong: *минуса три градуса); however: три минуса – three minuses.

linha.valor: For numbers above 1,000 Russian uses a modified short scale with the following loanwords: миллио́н (106, million; as for both long and short scales), миллиа́рд (109, milliard; as for long scale – an exception), триллио́н (1012, trillion), квадриллио́н (1015, quadrillion), квинтиллио́н (1018, quintillion), etc. (continued as short scale). They decline in the same way as миллио́н. Russian uses words биллио́н (billion) and numerals with -ard endings only in historical texts or literal translations. Also, биллиа́рд (billiard) is a noun meaning a cue sport.

linha.valor: Fractions +1⁄2, +1⁄3 and +1⁄4 have proper names (nouns): полови́на, треть and че́тверть, which are used instead of ordinal numbers. They are also often added with preposition с, while form of noun appears to be related to the integer part rather than to the fraction: де́сять с че́твертью [Instr.] оборо́тов [Gen.] "10+1⁄4 turns". Prefixes пол- (with Genitive) and полу- (with Nominative) are used for "half" of something: пол-лимо́на (half of a lemon), полчаса́ (half an hour; but: полови́на ча́са); полуме́сяц (half moon, crescent). Words with пол- are not declined, and there is a set of rules for writing with or without dash.

linha.valor: Ordinal numbers have grammatically no differences with adjectives. While forming them, upper three orders of numerals are agglutinated to nearest dividing power of 1000, which results in constructing some of the longest natural Russian words, e.g. стапятидесятитрёхты́сячный (153,000-th), while the next is сто пятьдеся́т три ты́сячи пе́рвый (153,001-st). In the latter example, only the last word is declined with noun.

linha.valor: Fractions are formed as: (how much parts), expressed by cardinal number in case of the phrase, plus (of how numerous parts), expressed by ordinal number; the construction is formed as like it were related to word часть "part" (grammatically feminine), which is usually omitted. Noun to such construction always comes in Genitive single, also as like it belonged to word часть: девяно́сто две пятидеся́тых то́нны "+92⁄50 tons". If an integer precedes a fraction, it is bound to it usually with the conjunction и, while the noun remains in Genitive: два и три восьмы́х оборо́та "2+3⁄8 turns" (оборо́т is masculine, so the numeral is два, not *две).

linha.valor: Fractions +1⁄2, +1⁄3 and +1⁄4 have proper names (nouns): полови́на, треть and че́тверть, which are used instead of ordinal numbers. They are also often added with preposition с, while form of noun appears to be related to the integer part rather than to the fraction: де́сять с че́твертью [Instr.] оборо́тов [Gen.] "10+1⁄4 turns". Prefixes пол- (with Genitive) and полу- (with Nominative) are used for "half" of something: пол-лимо́на (half of a lemon), полчаса́ (half an hour; but: полови́на ча́са); полуме́сяц (half moon, crescent). Words with пол- are not declined, and there is a set of rules for writing with or without dash.

linha.valor: Collective numerals (Russian: собира́тельные числи́тельные) are used in Russian (and many other Slavic languages) instead of usual cardinal ones in specific lexical and semantic situations. Russian collective numerals are different from the cardinal numerals in that the former emphasize ‘the totality’ or ‘the aggregate as a whole’, while the latter – ‘the individuated quantity’.[19] Only numerals from 2 (двое) to 7 (семеро) are actively used nowadays, while 8 to 10 are seldom used and 11–13 are not normative;[20] word о́ба (both) is also considered to be collective numeral.[19] In nominative and accusative, they always force the noun into genitive plural form (while their own accusative form is dependent on the animacy of the noun): трое друзей на охоту пошли, вижу двоих мужчин, вижу двое саней. (Three friends went hunting [together], I see two men [together], I see two sleighs [together].) These numerals are seldom used in oblique cases, especially instrumental.[20] A brief table of usage situations follows:

linha.valor: Fractions are formed as: (how much parts), expressed by cardinal number in case of the phrase, plus (of how numerous parts), expressed by ordinal number; the construction is formed as like it were related to word часть "part" (grammatically feminine), which is usually omitted. Noun to such construction always comes in Genitive single, also as like it belonged to word часть: девяно́сто две пятидеся́тых то́нны "+92⁄50 tons". If an integer precedes a fraction, it is bound to it usually with the conjunction и, while the noun remains in Genitive: два и три восьмы́х оборо́та "2+3⁄8 turns" (оборо́т is masculine, so the numeral is два, not *две).

linha.valor: Fractions +1⁄2, +1⁄3 and +1⁄4 have proper names (nouns): полови́на, треть and че́тверть, which are used instead of ordinal numbers. They are also often added with preposition с, while form of noun appears to be related to the integer part rather than to the fraction: де́сять с че́твертью [Instr.] оборо́тов [Gen.] "10+1⁄4 turns". Prefixes пол- (with Genitive) and полу- (with Nominative) are used for "half" of something: пол-лимо́на (half of a lemon), полчаса́ (half an hour; but: полови́на ча́са); полуме́сяц (half moon, crescent). Words with пол- are not declined, and there is a set of rules for writing with or without dash.

linha.valor: For "1+1⁄2" there is a special word полтора́ (feminine полторы́; in oblique cases полу́тора; requires Genitive): полтора́ я́блока – +3⁄2 apples. It can be used with larger numbers (полторы́ ты́сячи – 1 500, полтора миллио́на – 1 500 000) and, for approximate values, with smaller numbers (полтора деся́тка – ≈ 15, полторы со́тни – ≈ 150). There was also now-outdated form полтора́ста for exactly 150. As with other single-word numerals, it's possible to form nouns and multiplicative adjectives, associated with "1.5": полу́торка (old truck with 1.5 tonnes of payload capacity), полтора́шка (1.5 liter plastic bottle for beverage); полу́торный (something of 150% amount). Also (colloquially): полтора́ челове́ка "almost nobody" (lit. one and a half men).

linha.valor: To read decimal fractions,[note 3] convert them to simple ones: 2,71828 = 2 + +71828⁄100000 - два и се́мьдесят одна́ ты́сяча восемьсо́т два́дцать во́семь стоты́сячных. After integer in such cases is often used word це́лая (nominalized adjective "full, integer", which also refers to omitted word часть and thus is feminine): 3,14 – три це́лых (и) четы́рнадцать со́тых (union is often omitted); word це́лая can appear also in naming non-decimal simple fractions: 2+3⁄8 – две це́лых три восьмы́х. Zero before comma is often read: 0,01 = 0 + +1⁄100 – ноль це́лых одна́ со́тая (shortly: одна́ со́тая). Informally, decimal fractional part can be read more conveniently as sequence of simple digits and numbers: два и семь-восемна́дцать-два́дцать во́семь. Same method is used to read long numerals unrelated to a noun (phone numbers, address indexes, etc.), grouping two or three digits: 123406 – сто два́дцать три четы́реста шесть, двенадцать три́дцать четы́ре ноль шесть (forced ноль added to avoid missing digit).

linha.valor: Count form also exists for paucal numbers (1.5, 2, 3 and 4); usually it coincides with genitive singular, but has notable exceptions with stressed endings: два часа́ (2 hours), but середи́на ча́са (middle of an hour); два́дцать два шара́ (22 balls), but объём ша́ра (volume of the ball); три ряда́ (3 rows/lines), but вы́йти из ря́да (step out of the line); четы́ре шага́ (4 steps), but полша́га (half a step). Полчаса́ (half an hour) is additional exception; other nouns with пол- prefix does not have stressed -а ending.

russo.valor: Ита́к, неде́лю тому́ наза́д меня́ ски́нули с бригади́рства, а пять неде́ль тому́ наза́д — назна́чили. traducao.valor: So. A week ago I was kicked out of my job as brigade foreman, which I'd gotten five weeks ago. In four weeks, as you can understand, I couldn't have introduced any great changes, and even if anybody thought that I’d introduced any, all the same they didn’t sack me for great changes.

traducao.trecho: So. A week ago I was kicked out of my job as brigade foreman, which I'd gotten five weeks ago. notas_de_uso.valor: When the genitive plural is used after a cardinal number, the word лет (let, genitive plural of ле́то (léto, “summer”)) is used instead of годо́в (godóv). This applies to numbers whose names do not end in оди́н (odín, “one”), два (dva, “two”), три (tri, “three”), or четы́ре (četýre, “four”) when in the nominative, genitive, or accusative case (so this includes numbers like 114 whose name in Russian does not end in четы́ре), as well as to numbers ending in два (dva), три (tri), or четы́ре (četýre) in genitive case.

notas_de_uso.valor: To put this in another way, when a number should be followed by a nominative or genitive singular, the appropriate form of год (god) is used. linha.obs: título de subseção

linha.valor: The imperative mood second-person singular is formed from the future-present base of most verbs by adding -и (stressed ending in present-future, or if the base ends on more than one consonant), -ь (unstressed ending, base of one consonant) or -й (unstressed ending, base of vowel). The plural (including the polite на вы) second-person form is made by adding -те to the singular one: говорю 'I speak' – говори – говорите, забуду 'I shall forget' – забудь – забудьте, клею 'I glue' – клей – клейте. Some perfective verbs have a first-person plural imperative form with -те added to a similar simple future or present tense form: пойдёмте 'let us go'. Other forms can express commands in Russian; for third person, for example, the particle пусть with future can be used: Пусть они замолчат! 'Let them shut up!'.[20]

linha.valor: The conditional mood in Russian is formed by adding the particle бы after the word which marks the supposed subject into a sentence formed like in the past tense. Thus, to say "I would (hypothetically) sleep" or "I would like to sleep", a male speaker would say я спал бы (or я бы поспа́л), while a female speaker would say я спала́ бы (or я бы поспала́).

linha.valor: If the present stem ends in other consonant, the imperative ends in -и if the stress falls on the ending or in -ь if it falls on the stem: молч-у — молчи, сяд-у — сядь. Due to the positional changes of the consonants, the rule of thumb is to take the present stem from 3rd person plural: oтвеч-у — ответ-ят — ответь, нош-у — нос-ят — носи[13].

linha.valor: The Slavic languages lost the Proto-Indo-European subjunctive altogether, while the old optative was repurposed as the imperative mood. Some modern Slavic languages have developed a new subjunctive-like construction,[13][14] although there is no consistent terminology. For example, some authors do not distinguish the subjunctive mood from the optative ("wishing") mood,[15] while others do.[16]

linha.valor: Modal distinctions in subordinate clauses are expressed not through verb endings, but through the choice of complementizer – че (che) or да (da) (which might both be translated with the relative pronoun 'that'). The verbs remain unchanged. In ordinary sentences, the imperfective aspect is most often used for the indicative, and the perfective for the subjunctive, but any combination is possible, with the corresponding change in meaning. For example, iskam da stanesh (perfective) or iskam da stavash (imperfective) 'I want you to get up'. The latter is more insisting, since the imperfective is the more immediate construction. Thus:

linha.valor: The imperative mood second-person singular is formed from the future-present base of most verbs by adding -и (stressed ending in present-future, or if the base ends on more than one consonant), -ь (unstressed ending, base of one consonant) or -й (unstressed ending, base of vowel). The plural (including the polite на вы) second-person form is made by adding -те to the singular one: говорю 'I speak' – говори – говорите, забуду 'I shall forget' – забудь – забудьте, клею 'I glue' – клей – клейте. Some perfective verbs have a first-person plural imperative form with -те added to a similar simple future or present tense form: пойдёмте 'let us go'. Other forms can express commands in Russian; for third person, for example, the particle пусть with future can be used: Пусть они замолчат! 'Let them shut up!'.[20]

linha.valor: The Slavic languages lost the Proto-Indo-European subjunctive altogether, while the old optative was repurposed as the imperative mood. Some modern Slavic languages have developed a new subjunctive-like construction,[13][14] although there is no consistent terminology. For example, some authors do not distinguish the subjunctive mood from the optative ("wishing") mood,[15] while others do.[16]

linha.valor: The conditional mood in Russian is formed by adding the particle бы after the word which marks the supposed subject into a sentence formed like in the past tense. Thus, to say "I would (hypothetically) sleep" or "I would like to sleep", a male speaker would say я спал бы (or я бы поспа́л), while a female speaker would say я спала́ бы (or я бы поспала́).

For example, some authors do not distinguish the subjunctive mood from the optative ("wishing") mood,[15] while others do.[16]

linha.valor: Modal distinctions in subordinate clauses are expressed not through verb endings, but through the choice of complementizer – че (che) or да (da) (which might both be translated with the relative pronoun 'that'). The verbs remain unchanged. In ordinary sentences, the imperfective aspect is most often used for the indicative, and the perfective for the subjunctive, but any combination is possible, with the corresponding change in meaning. For example, iskam da stanesh (perfective) or iskam da stavash (imperfective) 'I want you to get up'. The latter is more insisting, since the imperfective is the more immediate construction. Thus:

notas_de_uso.valor: Unlike English because, Russian потому что can never govern an introductory clause (e.g. English "Because I was early, I had to wait"). For that, поско́льку (poskólʹku), та́к как (ták kak) and other conjunctions must be used. This separation of usage is not general to Russian conjunctions and is rather a peculiarity of a few including this one.
notas_de_uso.valor_texto: Unlike English because, Russian потому что can never govern an introductory clause (e.g. English "Because I was early, I had to wait"). For that, поско́льку (poskólʹku), та́к как (ták kak) and other conjunctions must be used. This separation of usage is not general to Russian conjunctions and is rather a peculiarity of a few including this one.
notas_de_uso.trecho: Unlike English because, Russian потому что can never govern an introductory clause (e.g. English "Because I was early, I had to wait"). For that, поско́льку (poskólʹku), та́к как (ták kak) and other conjunctions must be used. This separation of usage is not general to Russian conjunctions and is rather a peculiarity of a few including this one.

notas_de_uso.valor: Заче́м (Začém), while most often translated into English simply as "why" like почему́ (počemú), enquires about the goal/objective of something. It is quite often used in a similar manner to "what's the point of" (како́й смысл (kakój smysl)). Sometimes it is interchangeable with почему́ (počemú), but other times one is more appropriate than the other.

linha.valor: Unlike in standard English, multiple negatives are compulsory in Russian, as in "никто никогда никому ничего не прощает" [nʲɪkˈto nʲɪkɐɡˈda nʲɪkɐˈmu nʲɪtɕɪˈvo nʲɪ prɐˈɕ:æjɪt] ('No-one ever forgives anyone for anything' literally, "no one never to no-one nothing does not forgive"). Usually, only one word in a sentence has negative particle or prefix "не" or belongs to negative word "нет", while another word has negation-affirmative particle or prefix "ни"; but this word can often be omitted, and thus ни becomes the signal of negation: вокруг никого нет and вокруг никого both mean "there is nobody around".

linha.valor: No simple rule supplies an adverbial answer to a negative sentence. B. Comrie[33] says that in Russian answer да or нет is determined not so much by the negative form of the question as by the questioner's intent for using negation, or whether the response is in agreement with his presupposition. In many cases that means that the adverbial answer should be extended for avoiding ambiguity; in spoken language, intonation in saying нет can also be significant to if it is affirmation of negation or negation of negation.

linha.valor: Note that while expressing an affirmation of negation by extending "да" with a negated verb is grammatically acceptable. In practice it is more common to answer "нет" and subsequently extend with a negated verb paralleling the usage in English. Answering a negative sentence with a non-extended "нет" is usually interpreted as an affirmation of negation again in a way similar to English.

linha.valor: Conjoining coordinations are formed with the help of the conjunctions и "and", ни … ни ("not … not" — simultaneous negation), та́кже "also", то́же ("too"; the latter two have complementary flavors), etc. Most commonly the conjoining coordination expresses enumeration, simultaneity or immediate sequence. They may also have a cause-effect flavor.

linha.valor: The distinction between "и" and "а" developed after medieval times. Originally, "и" and "а" were closer in meaning. The unpunctuated ending of the Song of Igor illustrates the potential confusion. The final five words in modern spelling, "князьям слава а дружине аминь" [knʲɪˈzʲjam ˈslavə ɐ druˈʐɨnʲɪ ɐˈmʲinʲ] can be understood either as "Glory to the princes and to their retinue! Amen." or "Glory to the princes, and amen (R.I.P.) to their retinue". Although the majority opinion is definitely with the first interpretation, no consensus has formed. The psychological difference between the two is quite obvious.

linha.valor: Despite the inflectional nature of Russian, there is no equivalent in modern Russian to the English nominative absolute or the Latin ablative absolute construction. The old language had an absolute construction, with the noun in the dative. Like so many other archaisms, it is retained in Church Slavonic. Among the last known examples in literary Russian occurs in Radishchev's Journey from Petersburg to Moscow (Путешествие из Петербурга в Москву [pʊtʲɪˈʂɛstvʲɪje ɪs pʲɪtʲɪrˈburɡə v mɐˈskvu]), 1790:

linha.valor: Conjoining coordinations are formed with the help of the conjunctions и "and", ни … ни ("not … not" — simultaneous negation), та́кже "also", то́же ("too"; the latter two have complementary flavors), etc. Most commonly the conjoining coordination expresses enumeration, simultaneity or immediate sequence. They may also have a cause-effect flavor.

linha.valor: The distinction between "и" and "а" developed after medieval times. Originally, "и" and "а" were closer in meaning. The unpunctuated ending of the Song of Igor illustrates the potential confusion. The final five words in modern spelling, "князьям слава а дружине аминь" [knʲɪˈzʲjam ˈslavə ɐ druˈʐɨnʲɪ ɐˈmʲinʲ] can be understood either as "Glory to the princes and to their retinue! Amen." or "Glory to the princes, and amen (R.I.P.) to their retinue". Although the majority opinion is definitely with the first interpretation, no consensus has formed. The psychological difference between the two is quite obvious.

linha.valor: Unlike in standard English, multiple negatives are compulsory in Russian, as in "никто никогда никому ничего не прощает" [nʲɪkˈto nʲɪkɐɡˈda nʲɪkɐˈmu nʲɪtɕɪˈvo nʲɪ prɐˈɕ:æjɪt] ('No-one ever forgives anyone for anything' literally, "no one never to no-one nothing does not forgive"). Usually, only one word in a sentence has negative particle or prefix "не" or belongs to negative word "нет", while another word has negation-affirmative particle or prefix "ни"; but this word can often be omitted, and thus ни becomes the signal of negation: вокруг никого нет and вокруг никого both mean "there is nobody around".

linha.valor: No simple rule supplies an adverbial answer to a negative sentence. B. Comrie[33] says that in Russian answer да or нет is determined not so much by the negative form of the question as by the questioner's intent for using negation, or whether the response is in agreement with his presupposition. In many cases that means that the adverbial answer should be extended for avoiding ambiguity; in spoken language, intonation in saying нет can also be significant to if it is affirmation of negation or negation of negation.

linha.valor: Note that while expressing an affirmation of negation by extending "да" with a negated verb is grammatically acceptable. Answering a negative sentence with a non-extended "нет" is usually interpreted as an affirmation of negation again in a way similar to English.

linha.valor: Conjoining coordinations are formed with the help of the conjunctions и "and", ни … ни ("not … not" — simultaneous negation), та́кже "also", то́же ("too"; the latter two have complementary flavors), etc. Most commonly the conjoining coordination expresses enumeration, simultaneity or immediate sequence. They may also have a cause-effect flavor.
